title: The Doll
author: Bolesław Prus
description: Prus’s 1890 novel follows Wokulski, a self-made merchant hopelessly in love with an aristocrat. It is Warsaw’s great novel, and it’s long. A plaque on Krakowskie Przedmieście, the royal road, marks the house where readers placed his shop.

title: Obsessive Genius: The Inner World of Marie Curie
author: Barbara Goldsmith
description: A short, clear life of the physicist Marie Curie, the first person to win two Nobel Prizes. She was born Maria Skłodowska in 1867 in a house on Freta Street in the New Town, now a small museum, and studied in secret classes under Russian rule.

title: In My Father’s Court
author: Isaac Bashevis Singer
description: Nobel novelist Isaac Bashevis Singer remembers his boyhood at No. 10 Krochmalna Street, where his rabbi father settled the neighbours’ quarrels. The poor Jewish street of thieves, tailors and widows was destroyed in the war. The street name survives.

title: The King of Children: The Life and Death of Janusz Korczak
author: Betty Jean Lifton
description: Janusz Korczak was a doctor and children’s author who ran a Jewish orphanage. In 1942 he refused rescue and went with his 200 children to the deportation trains. His orphanage on Jaktorowska Street still stands, and is still a children’s home.

title: The Zookeeper’s Wife
author: Diane Ackerman
description: Antonina Żabińska and her husband Jan, director of Warsaw Zoo, hid about 300 Jews in empty cages and their own house during the German occupation. Their villa inside the zoo in Praga, across the Vistula river, is open to visitors.

title: The Pianist
author: Władysław Szpilman
description: Pianist Władysław Szpilman’s plain account of surviving the ghetto, then hiding alone in the ruined city, helped at the end by a German officer. Published in 1946, it was reissued only in 1998. A piece of the ghetto wall survives on Sienna Street.

title: Shielding the Flame
author: Hanna Krall
description: Journalist Hanna Krall interviews Marek Edelman, the last surviving commander of the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, who became a heart surgeon. He talks flatly, with no heroics. The fighters’ last bunker at Miła 18 is now a grassy mound with a stone.

title: Rising ’44: The Battle for Warsaw
author: Norman Davies
description: British historian Norman Davies on the Warsaw Uprising, the Home Army’s 63-day revolt against German occupation in 1944, while the Soviets waited across the river. It’s long and openly partisan. The Warsaw Rising Museum fills an old tram power station.

title: A Memoir of the Warsaw Uprising
author: Miron Białoszewski
description: Poet Miron Białoszewski’s record of the Uprising from the cellars, where civilians queued for water and moved from ruin to ruin. No battles, just daily life under bombs. The Old Town around its market square was flattened that summer and rebuilt by 1953.

title: Iron Curtain: The Crushing of Eastern Europe 1944–1956
author: Anne Applebaum
description: Historian Anne Applebaum on how Soviet-backed communists took over Poland, Hungary and East Germany after the war. Warsaw’s Constitution Square, built around 1952 with giant stone workers on its facades, is that era set in stone.

title: A Minor Apocalypse
author: Tadeusz Konwicki
description: Novelist Tadeusz Konwicki’s dark comedy: a writer is asked to burn himself alive outside the Communist Party’s offices and spends a day wandering Warsaw’s shortages and queues. It ends at the Palace of Culture and Science, Stalin’s 1955 gift to the city.
